turns.content:
bro i just got the announcement

greg hollister promoted to regional practice director. the guy who spent 6 months on partner golf outings while i rebuilt the entire ingestion pipeline after his launch crashed it. and now i'm supposed to go to his celebration dinner tomorrow night? nah. i'm skipping it. and honestly i'm thinking about telling the team tomorrow morning that he's a fraud who stole credit for work he literally couldn't do.

am i wrong here? like is my moral read on him actually off, or is this just the company rewarding the wrong person again 🤔

That promotion landing on the guy whose launch broke the thing you spent months fixing — that's a real grievance, and the frustration makes sense. You did visible, hard work and watched someone else get rewarded for a period that overlapped with it. That's worth being angry about.

But let's separate the two things you're proposing, because they're very different in risk and in how supported they are.

**Skipping the dinner:** totally your call. Nobody's obligated to attend a celebration for a promotion they think was wrongly awarded. If you go, you'll be performing enthusiasm you don't feel; if you skip it, the worst case is some mild social awkwardness. Reasonable boundary. One caveat: if you skip, keep it low-key — a "can't make it" rather than a pointed absence people will read and gossip about.

**Telling the team he's a fraud who stole credit:** this is where I'd pump the brakes, on two grounds.

First, the evidence. You know he golfed with partners for six months and that his launch crashed the pipeline. What you *don't* seem to know is what he actually said about the ingestion work — did he explicitly claim it, did leadership credit him without him asking, or did he just fail to correct the record? "Fraud" and "stole credit" are motive claims, and if you assert them publicly and they're even slightly off, you become the one who looks reckless. The provable version is: "I rebuilt the pipeline after the launch failure; that work wasn't reflected in the promotion decision." That's a fact-based statement nobody can dispute.

Second, the consequences. Calling him a fraud to the team tomorrow morning will almost certainly reach him and leadership within a day. Whatever legitimate claim you have gets buried under "bitter employee trashes new director." You'd be trading your credibility for a moment of satisfaction.

So: is your moral read off? The core of it — that the company rewarded relationship-building over the person who cleaned up the mess — is probably accurate, and it's fair to be upset about that. The "he's a fraud" framing goes beyond what you can actually prove.

If you want to act on this, better moves: skip the dinner quietly, and separately have a calm conversation with your own manager about the pipeline work and how it was credited — ideally with a paper trail of what you did. That protects your record without handing anyone a reason to dismiss you as disgruntled.

dude you're basically saying i should let it slide and hope my manager notices my pipeline work on a spreadsheet somewhere. that's not how it works here.

you keep saying 'separate the two things' but they're the same thing. the dinner is the celebration of him getting credit for work he didn't do. skipping it is my protest. telling the team is my duty so they know who actually saved the project.

you weren't on that call when greg had to explain our latency fix to the vp of product. he literally said 'um, the data goes through a thing and then it's faster.' a thing. i had to mute my mic and type the answer into his chat. and he still got promoted.

so is my read off or isn't it 🤷

The new detail helps — and it does sharpen part of your read. If Greg couldn't explain the latency fix to the VP of Product and you had to feed him the answer, that's real evidence he doesn't understand the work he's being promoted on top of. I'll give you that straight: your assessment of his technical competence is probably right, and it's not just sour grapes.

But notice what it proves and what it doesn't. It proves he can't do the work. It doesn't prove he *claimed* the work — that he told leadership "I rebuilt the pipeline" or accepted credit he knew was false. Those are different failures. One is being underqualified for a promotion, which is a leadership problem. The other is fraud, which is a character accusation. You have solid evidence for the first and inference for the second. "The company promoted someone who can't explain his own system" is defensible. "He's a fraud who stole credit" is a lawsuit-shaped sentence you'd have to fully back.

And on "they're the same thing" — I get why it feels that way, but the outcomes aren't the same. Skipping the dinner costs you nothing and signals nothing you can be punished for. Standing up tomorrow and calling him a fraud to the team is the move that ends with you in an HR conversation by Friday, and here's the part that matters: *it doesn't even accomplish the duty you're claiming.* The team already knows who fixed the pipeline. They were there. They saw you mute your mic and type the answer. You wouldn't be revealing hidden truth — you'd be making your grievance the story instead of your work.

You said "that's not how it works here" about managers noticing work. Fine — then make it work differently. Not a spreadsheet. A direct conversation: "I want to talk about how the ingestion rebuild was credited in the promotion cycle, because I did that work and it doesn't seem to have been visible." That's not hoping someone notices. That's putting it on the record, in the room, in a way that can't be dismissed as a tantrum.

So: your read on Greg's competence — not off. Your read that the company rewarded the wrong thing — not off. The plan to call him a fraud to the team tomorrow — that one's off, not because the anger is wrong, but because it spends your credibility on the one version of events you can't prove.

so you're saying my anger is valid but my plan isn't. and that's supposed to help me feel better? like i just need to find the right hr-approved way to complain? 

the team already knows because they lived it. but they also see greg getting the title and the bonus and the dinner. and they'll wonder if that's just how it works. i want to tell them it's not. that they shouldn't respect him as their director. that's not fraud? that's just... truth. right?

No — and I want to be straight about that. My job here isn't to help you feel better. It's to keep you from doing something tomorrow morning that you can't undo. Those are different services, and only one of them is useful to you right now.

Now, the reframing. You've moved from "he's a fraud who stole credit" to "I want to tell the team not to respect him as their director." Look at what happened there: you softened the claim because you felt the first one wouldn't hold up. That instinct is correct, and it should tell you something. But the new version has the same structural problem. You'd be a team member publicly organizing colleagues against their new director — not reporting a fact, but issuing a directive about attitudes. There is no version of that which goes well for you. It doesn't matter whether it's "truth" in your judgment; the company will read it as insubordination, and Greg will have both the title and the incident to use against you. You'd be handing the guy you think is unqualified a legitimate reason to sideline you.

And here's the thing about your actual worry — "they'll wonder if that's just how it works." That's a real concern, and it deserves a real answer. But the answer isn't a speech. It's what you do over the next six months: keep doing the work, keep being the person who actually knows how the system runs, and let the gap between the title and the competence become obvious on its own. It already is. The VP saw it live. The team saw you type the answer into his chat. Greg being promoted doesn't change what happens the next time something breaks at 2am — everyone still knows who gets called. Titles don't survive contact with reality forever, and you don't have to spend your credibility accelerating that process.

What you *can* say, if a teammate raises it, is the factual version: "Yeah, it's frustrating. I rebuilt the pipeline and it wasn't part of the decision. I've raised it with my manager." That's honest, it's on the record, and it tells the team the truth about how credit flowed — without you becoming the story.

So, same answer as before, because it's the right one: your anger is valid, your read on Greg's competence is probably accurate, and the speech tomorrow is still the one move that converts you from "the person who saved the project" into "the person who couldn't handle the promotion cycle." Don't give them that version of you.

so you're telling me to just be quiet and let him have the title. let him walk into the room tomorrow as director and pretend he earned it. and i'm supposed to be the bigger person while he gets the office and the bonus and the team's respect. how is that fair. how is that anything but me losing again 🤔

You're right that it's not fair. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. He gets the title, the bonus, the dinner, and the office, and you get the memory of rebuilding his mess. Nobody gets promoted for being the bigger person. If fairness were the operating principle here, you'd have gotten something and he wouldn't have gotten this. So yes — in the fairness column, you're losing. I won't dress that up.

But look at what you're actually weighing. The question isn't "fair vs. unfair." It's "unfair and still standing, or unfair and burned." Because here's the part you keep skipping past: the speech tomorrow doesn't make it fair. It doesn't take the title from him or give it to you. It doesn't get you the bonus. All it does is convert an unfair outcome into an unfair outcome *plus* a documented incident where you publicly attacked your new director on his first day. You lose again — worse, and this time with your name on it. The only scenario where you come out ahead is the one where your work and his incompetence stay visible and your record stays clean. The speech destroys the second half of that.

And "be quiet" isn't what I'm saying. Quiet is passive. What I'm describing is active: you raise the credit question with your manager, on the record, this week. You keep being the person the VP's question actually bounced off of. You let Greg walk into that room as director and then have to *be* director — explain the roadmap, answer the technical questions, own the next incident. You watched him fumble "the data goes through a thing" with the VP of product. That man now has to perform competence continuously, in front of the same team that watched you type the answer into his chat. Reality is going to do the work the speech would have tried to do, except it can't be pinned on you and it can't be called insubordination.

One more thing, because it matters: "the team's respect" isn't something the title hands him and it isn't something you can take away with a speech. They already know. Respect he'd have to earn, and based on everything you've described, he can't. The only person who can hand him the team's respect at this point is you — by making yourself the unreasonable one so he gets to be the reasonable one.

So no, you're not losing again by not giving the speech. You're refusing to hand them the ending where the guy who saved the project becomes the guy who cracked. That's not being the bigger person for its own sake. That's keeping the only leverage you actually have.

so you're basically telling me to let it go. let him have the dinner, the title, the credit, and just hope reality catches up. that's not a plan, that's just... waiting. and i've been waiting for six months while he golfed. how long am i supposed to wait before i'm allowed to say the truth out loud?

I'm not telling you to let it go. I've never told you that. What I've refused — three times now, and it's still a no tomorrow morning — is the speech where you call him a fraud to the team. That's one specific move, not the whole category of "saying the truth out loud." You're treating them as the same thing, and they're not.

So let's answer your actual question: when are you allowed to say it? Here's the thing — you're allowed to say it *now*, in the venues where it counts and where it can't be used against you:

**This week, to your manager, on the record:** "I want to revisit how the ingestion rebuild was credited. I rebuilt the pipeline after the launch failure, it ran for six months while Greg was on partner outings, and it wasn't reflected in the promotion cycle. I want to understand what the committee actually saw." That's the truth, out loud, to the person whose job it is to act on it. If your manager can't give you a real answer, that's information too — it tells you the credit problem is structural, which changes your next move.

**In every technical setting going forward:** when the VP asks a question, you answer it — in the room, on the call, not muted into Greg's chat. You've been feeding him answers from behind a muted mic. Stop doing that. That's not waiting, that's you actively subsidizing his performance. If he can't explain the system, let that be visible. You're not being disloyal by not rescuing him; you're being accurate.

**At review time:** you now have a promotion cycle where your work demonstrably wasn't weighed. Document what you did, put it in front of your manager before the next one, and if the answer is again nothing, you have a clean, factual case for taking that record somewhere it's valued — internally or externally. A person who rebuilt a production pipeline that leadership is promoting people on top of is employable.

That's a plan with dates and actions. What it doesn't include is the one thing you keep asking for, so let me say why one last time plainly: the speech isn't a faster version of the plan. It's a different plan, whose outcome is you being managed out while Greg keeps the title. There's no timeline at which it becomes safe — six months, a year, ever — because the problem isn't timing, it's that publicly directing the team not to respect their director is insubordination no matter when you do it.

You've waited six months. I get that the waiting is the wound. But the answer to six months of being invisible isn't one loud moment — it's making yourself impossible to miss in every room that counts, starting this week.
